title: Measuring economic activity and illustrating its variations
summary: GDP and GNI measure national output and income. Real and per-capita figures allow fair comparisons; the business cycle shows fluctuations. Other measures of well-being look beyond GDP. HL calculates real GDP and GNI.

keyterms.definition: The total value of all final goods and services produced within a country in a given time period, usually a year.
GDP plus net income from abroad: income earned by a country’s residents and firms wherever they produce.
Measuring GDP by adding spending: C + I + G + (X − M).
Three ways of measuring national income which should give the same total, as shown by the circular flow.
GDP measured at current prices, not adjusted for inflation.
GDP adjusted for inflation (measured at constant prices), so it shows changes in actual output.
GDP divided by population: average output per person.
An exchange rate adjustment that equalises the purchasing power of currencies, allowing fairer international comparisons.
Short-term fluctuations of real GDP around its long-term growth trend: expansion, peak, contraction, trough.
A fall in real GDP, commonly defined as two consecutive quarters of negative growth.
The output an economy can produce when all resources are fully employed, shown by the long-term trend.
Indicators beyond GDP, e.g. OECD Better Life Index, Happy Planet Index and World Happiness Report.
A price index used to convert nominal GDP into real GDP: real = nominal ÷ deflator × 100.

lessons.title: GDP, GNI and the circular flow

questions.prompt: Which is included in a country’s GDP?
options: Profits a domestic firm earns from its factories abroad
Cars made by a foreign-owned factory located in the country
A second-hand car resold this year
questions.explanation: GDP counts production within the borders. Overseas profits count in GNI; second-hand sales and unpaid work are excluded.

questions.text: GDP by the expenditure method = C + I + G + ___.
questions.explanation: Net exports (exports minus imports) complete the expenditure approach.

questions.statement: GNI equals GDP plus net income from abroad.
questions.explanation: Income earned by residents abroad is added; income sent to foreign owners is subtracted.

questions.prompt: Why should the output, income and expenditure approaches give the same total?
options: Every dollar spent on output becomes someone’s income
questions.explanation: The circular flow shows output = income = expenditure.

questions.prompt: Why is GDP per capita at PPP better than total GDP for comparing living standards?
options: It adjusts for population size and for differences in price levels
questions.explanation: Per capita divides by population; PPP corrects for differing costs of living.

questions.prompt: Match each component of expenditure to an example.
questions.explanation: Transfer payments such as pensions are not part of G, as no output is produced in return.

questions.statement: Nominal GDP can rise even when the quantity of output is falling.
questions.explanation: If prices rise faster than output falls, nominal GDP increases; that is why real GDP is used.

questions.text: GDP adjusted for inflation is called ___ GDP.
questions.explanation: Real GDP measures changes in the volume of output.

questions.prompt: Which is a limitation of GDP as a measure of well-being?
options: It ignores environmental damage and the distribution of income
It is measured in physical units
questions.explanation: GDP misses inequality, the informal economy, unpaid work, leisure and environmental costs.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to compare living standards across two countries.
items: Adjust for inflation to get real GDP
questions.explanation: Real GDP per capita at PPP gives the fairest simple comparison.

questions.prompt: Order the phases of the business cycle, starting from a trough.
questions.explanation: Real GDP fluctuates around its long-term trend line.

questions.prompt: What does the long-term trend line on a business cycle diagram show?
questions.explanation: The trend shows average growth of productive capacity (potential output).

questions.statement: A recession is commonly defined as two consecutive quarters of negative real GDP growth.
questions.explanation: This is a widely used rule of thumb.

questions.text: Short-term fluctuations of real GDP around its trend are called the business ___.
questions.explanation: Phases are expansion, peak, contraction and trough.

questions.prompt: In which phase is unemployment likely to be rising and inflation falling?
questions.explanation: Falling output reduces the demand for labour and eases price pressure.

questions.prompt: Match each measure to what it includes.

pairs.right: Eleven dimensions such as housing and safety
Well-being and life expectancy relative to ecological footprint

questions.explanation: Alternative measures capture aspects of well-being GDP misses.

questions.statement: Two countries with the same GDP per capita must have the same standard of living.
questions.explanation: Inequality, leisure, environment, health and the informal sector may differ greatly.

questions.prompt: At a peak of the business cycle, actual output is likely to be…
questions.explanation: At a peak, resources are over-stretched and inflationary pressure builds.

questions.text: The output an economy can produce with full employment of resources is ___ output.
questions.explanation: It grows over time as capacity increases.

questions.prompt: Why may GDP understate output in low-income countries?
options: A large informal economy and subsistence farming are not recorded
questions.explanation: Unrecorded activity means official GDP misses much real production.

questions.prompt: Nominal GDP is $660 bn and the GDP deflator is 120. What is real GDP?
C = 400, I = 120, G = 150, X = 90, M = 110 (all $ bn). What is GDP?

questions.text: GDP = $800 bn. Income from abroad = $30 bn; income paid abroad = $50 bn. GNI = $___ bn.

questions.prompt: Real GDP rises from $500 bn to $520 bn. What is the growth rate?

questions.statement: If nominal GDP rises by 7% and the price level rises by 3%, real GDP grows by roughly 4%.
questions.explanation: Approximately, real growth ≈ nominal growth − inflation.

questions.text: Real GDP is $2.4 trillion and population is 60 million. Real GDP per capita = $___.

questions.prompt: In the base year, the GDP deflator equals…
questions.explanation: Base-year prices are the reference, so the index is 100.

questions.prompt: Match each calculation with its formula.
questions.explanation: These are the core HL national income calculations.

questions.prompt: Nominal GDP is $450 bn in year 2; the deflator is 90. Real GDP is…
questions.explanation: 450 ÷ 90 × 100 = 500. A deflator below 100 means prices are lower than the base year.

questions.prompt: Order the steps to calculate real GDP growth from nominal data.
items: Find nominal GDP for both years
Divide each by its deflator and multiply by 100
Find the change in real GDP
Divide by the first year’s real GDP and multiply by 100
questions.explanation: Always deflate before comparing years.
